name: Misunderstanding the assignment
object_raw: Thesis — turn a topic into a contestable claim that answers the assignment
bottleneck: draft is a topic (school is important) rather than a claim (year-round school would/would not help students learn); does not answer the assignment.
diagnosed: no thesis / controlling claim present
draft does not answer the assignment question
no position on year-round school
evidence: draft stays at topic level; no evaluative language about year-round school
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around one central claim, and could a reader restate it?
next: once a position is stated, scope it and connect it to supporting reasons
coaching: You've already put something real on the page — your draft shows you genuinely believe school matters and connects to students' futures, and that conviction is exactly the raw material a strong argument is built from. Essays are constructed from a few elements that work together — a central claim, the reasons behind it, and the evidence that supports those reasons — and today we're focusing on your thesis, the part that tells your reader the single main idea your whole essay exists to establish. A thesis does one specific job: it takes a topic and turns it into a position your reader can understand, agree with, or push back against. One strategy writers use when building a thesis is to ask themselves, "What is the most important idea I want my reader to accept?" — and then shape the answer into one focused, direct statement. Your draft tells us school is important, but it hasn't yet answered the assignment's actual question: would year-round school help students learn? Try finishing this thought in your own words: *Year-round school would [help / not help] students learn because…* Once your thesis stakes out a clear position, we'll come back to scope it further and connect it to your supporting reasons.

name: Answering a broader question than asked
object_raw: Thesis — reorient to assignment scope (teen friendships)
bottleneck: thesis addresses society broadly, not teen friendships — does not answer the assignment.
diagnosed: thesis does not answer the assignment (says 'society' not 'teen friendships')

no essay body yet to develop

next: once thesis addresses teen friendships, check that the claim is contestable and appropriately scoped.
coaching: You've already done something real here: you've taken a clear position and committed to it, which is exactly the move a writer needs to make. Now let's focus on your **thesis** — the single sentence that tells your reader the one main idea your whole essay exists to establish and defend. An essay is built from a few parts working together (a claim, the reasons behind it, the evidence that supports it), and the thesis sits at the center of all of them, giving every paragraph its direction. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves: *What is the most important idea I want my reader to understand or accept?* — and then shape that answer into one focused, specific statement. Right now your draft argues that social media is bad for society broadly, but the assignment is asking you to zoom in on one specific relationship: whether social media harms friendships among teens. Can you write one sentence that takes a clear position on that question — whether social media does or doesn't harm teen friendships — using your own words? Once your thesis is aimed at that specific claim, we'll look at whether it's contestable and scoped in a way that your essay can fully support.

name: No thesis
object_raw: Thesis — turning the topic into a contestable claim
bottleneck: topic present; claim absent — reader cannot tell what the writer thinks or what the essay will argue.
diagnosed: thesis absent — topic not claim
communicative purpose unestablished
no contestable position taken

student recognizes multiple perspectives exist
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around one central claim, and could a reader restate it?
next: once a contestable claim is formed, scope it to what the essay can support.
coaching: You've already done something important: you've identified a real, debated topic and acknowledged that people genuinely disagree about it — that sense of tension is exactly where a strong essay begins. Now let's work on your thesis, which is the one sentence that tells your reader the main idea your whole essay is trying to establish and prove. An essay is built from a few structural elements that work together — a thesis, the reasons behind it, and the evidence that supports those reasons — and the thesis is the spine everything else hangs on; without it, a reader finishes your opening not knowing what you actually think. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves: *What is the most important idea I want my reader to understand or accept?* — then turn that answer into a focused, direct statement, not just a description of the topic. Right now your sentences tell us *that* people have opinions about homework, but they don't yet tell us *yours* — so here's your move: what do YOU think should happen with homework, and why would a thoughtful person who disagrees with you see it differently? name: Topic mistaken for thesis
object_raw: Thesis — turning topic into contestable claim
bottleneck: draft is a topic announcement, not a claim; reader cannot tell what the essay will argue.
diagnosed: topic-not-claim: draft names a subject with no position
announcement pattern: 'i will talk about...' replaces thesis
evidence: 'whether they are good or bad' shows awareness of two sides
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around one central claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: once a contestable claim exists, check scope and connect to body organization.
coaching: You've done something every writer has to do first — you've named your subject and signaled to your reader that a position is coming, which gives your essay a clear starting point to build from. Now let's work on your thesis, the single sentence that tells your reader the one main idea your whole essay exists to establish and defend. A thesis isn't just a topic — it's a claim, the part of your essay that takes a position a thoughtful reader could actually push back on or disagree with, and everything else in your essay will exist to support it. One strategy writers use here is to ask themselves: "What is the most important idea I want my reader to understand or accept by the end?" — and then shape the answer into one focused, supportable statement. Once your thesis is strong, it becomes the organizing spine of your whole essay: your introduction, your supporting paragraphs, and even your word choices all grow out of that one central claim. So here's your next move: try finishing this sentence in your own words — *School uniforms are _______ because _______* — and aim for something a reasonable person could argue against. After we've sharpened that claim, we'll look at how to connect it to the body of your essay.

name: Vague thesis
object_raw: Thesis — move from topic/both-sides statement to a contestable claim
bottleneck: topic_not_claim — sentence names the issue and two sides but asserts nothing a reader could dispute.
diagnosed: topic-not-claim: sentence names issue without asserting a position
both-sides framing avoids commitment required by argumentative assignment
evidence: sentence names the assignment topic — student is on task.
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around one central claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: once a contestable claim is formed, check its scope and whether it answers the full assignment.
coaching: You've already identified something real in your opening — you can see that this issue has genuine tension and that there are meaningful reasons on both sides, and that awareness is actually a strong foundation to build from. Now let's focus on your thesis, which is the single sentence that tells your reader the one main idea your whole essay exists to establish and defend. Right now your sentence names the topic and signals complexity, but it doesn't yet land on a position — a reader finishes it still unsure what you actually think cities should do. A thesis works together with everything else in your essay: your introduction sets it up, your body paragraphs exist to support it, and your reader uses it to understand where you're taking them. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves, "What is the most important idea I want my reader to walk away convinced of?" — then turn that answer into a focused, supportable statement rather than a survey of the debate. Try completing this sentence in your own words: *Cities should (or should not) ban cars downtown because ___* — what's the position you most want a reader to accept? Once your thesis stakes out a clear claim, we'll look at its scope and make sure it fully answers the assignment.

name: Adequate thesis
object_raw: Supporting Claim — first body paragraph assertion that advances the thesis
bottleneck: thesis exists but no supporting assertion yet; student must now move from the central claim to one contributing step of the argument
diagnosed: thesis is sufficient — exit criterion met; move to supporting claims
no body paragraphs exist — first supporting claim is the developmental edge
student has not yet demonstrated ability to turn a reason into an assertive contributing claim
evidence: thesis is arguable and directly answers the assignment
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: can the student state one assertion that contributes a distinct step toward the central claim?
next: student states a first supporting claim; then develop evidence for it
coaching: Your thesis does exactly what a strong thesis should — it makes a clear, contestable claim that a reader can either agree or push back on: that test scores measure family income more than a student's ability to succeed. That gives your whole essay a job to do. Now we're ready to move into your first body paragraph, and the key building block there is a **supporting claim** — a single assertion that takes one step toward proving your thesis is true, not just a topic or an area you'll discuss. Essays are built from a few structural elements working together: a thesis that states the central idea, and then supporting claims that each advance it, paragraph by paragraph. One strategy writers use here is to ask, *What is one reason a reader should believe my thesis?* — and then write the answer as a direct, arguable statement rather than an open-ended subject. Look back at your thesis and ask yourself: what is ONE specific reason standardized tests track income more than ability? Write that reason as a full assertion — your own words, your own reasoning. Once you have that first supporting claim on the page, we'll work on bringing in evidence to back it up.

name: Strong thesis that should not be over-taught
object_raw: Thesis — consolidate the emerging controlling idea so the student has a conscious decision rule before continuing
bottleneck: the thesis is present and strong but not yet consciously consolidated as a governing decision rule — the student may continue drafting without a clear anchor.
diagnosed: confirm and consolidate the governing thesis before drafting continues
note that context/background for a naive reader is absent — a future opportunity
scope of the claim (does 'our old collaboration' / 'proximity mistaken for teamwork' need definition?) — minor, defer
evidence: sentence 1 is contestable and specific
sentence 2 converts the claim into a principle — a strong organizational move
strategy: brief consolidation of what the student has learned
connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around this one central claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it? — yes, substantially met.
next: return to drafting with confirmed governing claim; next body paragraph will need to develop the proximity/teamwork distinction with evidence and explanation.
coaching: Your two opening sentences are doing something genuinely strong: the first makes a claim a thoughtful reader could push back on, and the second sharpens it into a transferable principle — that's exactly the kind of intellectual move that anchors an essay. You've essentially already built your thesis, which is the structural element we're focused on right now — the part that tells your reader the single main idea the whole essay exists to establish, and that everything else in the essay will exist to develop and support. A thesis works at the center of your essay's architecture, giving your introduction its direction, orienting your reader, and acting as a decision rule: if a paragraph doesn't serve this claim, it doesn't belong. One strategy writers use at this stage is to ask themselves, *What is the single most important idea I want my reader to accept by the end?* — and then write the answer as one focused, supportable sentence. Try that now: in one sentence, state the idea you most want your reader to walk away convinced of — this will confirm your governing claim and give you a clear test for every paragraph you draft next. Once you have that sentence, you'll be ready to move into your body paragraphs, where you'll need to develop the distinction you've named — between proximity and actual teamwork — with evidence and explanation.

name: Evidence without explanation
object_raw: Explanation — adding at least one sentence that interprets the 20% statistic and connects it to the claim
bottleneck: evidence and claim sit adjacent with no reasoning step — the classic 'no_reasoning' case from common_difficulties.
diagnosed: explanation entirely absent — no interpretive link between evidence and claim
controlling idea / topic sentence is bare ('phones hurt learning' names a topic, not a full contribution)
paragraph closure missing
evidence: two relevant statistics are present — student understands evidence is needed.
claim is stated up front — student has some sense of paragraph structure.
exit: the reader can understand why the evidence supports the claim — i.e., at least one interpretive sentence is present.
next: draft one interpretive sentence connecting the 20% statistic to the claim; then extend to the second statistic.
coaching: You've already done two important things: you've made a clear claim — phones hurt learning — and you've backed it up with real evidence, including that striking 20% test-score gap. An essay is built from a few elements that work together — a central claim, the evidence behind it, and the explanations that connect them — and today we're focusing on explanation, the writing move that shows your reader *how* your evidence actually supports your claim. Explanation is the bridge between a fact and an argument: without it, your reader sees the statistic but has to guess why it matters. A strategy writers use is to ask two questions in sequence: *What does this evidence show?* and then *How does that help establish my claim?* — working through those two questions one at a time keeps the reasoning clear and transferable to any essay you write. Try it now: after your 20% statistic, write one sentence in your own words that answers those two questions — what that number reveals, and why it means phones are hurting learning. Once your reader can follow that connection clearly, you'll have a strong explanation pattern to bring to your second statistic as well.

name: Explanation without evidence
object_raw: Evidence — scaffolding the student toward identifying one concrete, specific ground for the claim
bottleneck: student conflates personal conviction and assumed consensus with evidence; no concrete, checkable information is present.
diagnosed: no evidence present — highest-leverage gap for 'ground reasoning in evidence' telos
topic sentence announces topic but does not make a contestable, developed claim
explanation entirely absent — but premature until evidence exists
sentence 3 ('everyone knows') undermines credibility
evidence: opening sentence states a clear position — shows understanding that argument requires a stance.
exit: can the claim now be reasonably accepted or considered by the reader? (evidence exit) — not yet met.
next: student names one concrete ground; then teach evidence-to-claim connection (explanation).
coaching: You've already done something important: you've planted a clear central claim — that keeping animals in captivity is wrong — and that gives your essay a real position to build from. Now we're going to work on evidence, which is the part of an essay that gives your reader actual reasons to believe that claim. Evidence isn't a feeling or something "everyone knows" — it's concrete information a skeptical reader could look at, weigh, and consider for themselves, and it works alongside your claim and your explanation to make your argument genuinely persuasive. One strategy writers use is to ask: what does my claim require the reader to believe, and what specific information would give them a reason to believe it? So here's your move: think about one concrete, specific thing you actually know about zoos and animals in captivity — something a doubtful reader could check or consider — and write it down in your own words. Once you've named that concrete ground, we'll work on connecting it back to your claim so your reader can see exactly why it matters.

name: Irrelevant evidence
object_raw: Evidence relevance — identifying that the cafeteria sentence does not support the recess claim
bottleneck: student has not yet distinguished evidence that supports the recess-length claim from evidence that supports a different claim (school nutrition). relevance dimension is the gap.
diagnosed: evidence relevance: cafeteria sentence is off-claim
explanation missing: heart-health sentence not connected to claim
topic sentence/controlling idea absent as a focused claim
paragraph purpose diffuse (two unrelated topics)
evidence: heart-health sentence is topically connected to exercise/recess
student did produce a recognizable claim-support structure

coaching: You've already done something real here: you made a clear claim — recess should be longer — and then backed it up with a fact about exercise and heart health, which connects directly to what happens during recess. That's a writer making moves. An essay is built from a few working parts — your central claim, the reasons behind it, and the evidence that supports those reasons — and today we're focusing on **evidence relevance**: whether each piece of information you've chosen actually supports your specific claim. Evidence gives your reader reasons to believe *that claim* — not a nearby idea, but *this* one. A useful strategy writers use is to pause at each piece of evidence and ask: "What does my claim need the reader to believe, and does this information give them a reason to believe it?" Your heart-health sentence passes that test pretty well, since recess is a time for exercise. So look at your cafeteria sentence: does the fact that school food isn't healthy give your reader a reason to believe recess should be *longer*, or is it really about something else? Once you've worked that out, we'll turn to your heart-health evidence and look at how to explain the connection between it and your claim more fully.

name: Weak paragraph unity
object_raw: Unity — identifying which sentences serve the paragraph's governing purpose and which do not
bottleneck: student applies an 'on-topic' test rather than an 'on-purpose' test — keeping sentences because they relate to the revolution, not because they develop the explanation of taxation as a cause.
diagnosed: unity: three sentences do not serve the paragraph's governing purpose
topic sentence: sentences 1–2 together gesture at a controlling idea but no single sentence names it clearly
supporting detail: boston tea party mention could develop the controlling idea if connected; currently unexplained
evidence: sentences 1–2 share a governing idea and cohere around taxation as cause
exit: can the paragraph be understood as accomplishing one identifiable purpose? (paragraph purpose exit criterion)
next: once student identifies off-purpose sentences, develop the controlling idea into a clear topic sentence.
coaching: Your first two sentences are already doing real work — "Taxes were a big cause of the revolution" and "The colonists were mad about taxes without representation" point your reader toward the same idea, and that focus is exactly what strong writing builds on. Today we're working on **unity** — the idea that every sentence in a paragraph should serve the paragraph's one job for the reader. A paragraph has a purpose, which means it has something you want your reader to understand or believe by the end; unity happens when every sentence you write pushes toward that same change in the reader's mind. One strategy writers use to check for unity is to ask, "What should my reader understand after finishing this?" and then hold each sentence up against that answer — if a sentence doesn't help deliver that understanding, it's pulling the paragraph in a different direction. This matters because a unified paragraph feeds your thesis, shapes your reader's attention, and keeps your organization from drifting. So look at your last three sentences — "George Washington was a great general," "The Boston Tea Party happened," and "Britain was far away across the ocean" — and using your first two sentences as your guide, can you tell me which of those three is actually helping explain why taxes caused colonial anger, and which ones seem to be about something else?

name: Missing topic sentence
object_raw: Topic Sentence — student must state the paragraph's contribution as a claim
bottleneck: paragraph presents topic information (events) without asserting what they contribute — topic_not_claim difficulty
diagnosed: no topic sentence / governing claim
no interpretation of evidence
no connection to thesis or theme
final sentence ('these are all in the book') adds nothing
evidence: three events are all from one chapter, suggesting intentional selection around a point
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: can the remaining sentences reasonably develop a governing idea? — not yet met
next: use the student's claim to draft a topic sentence that governs the paragraph
coaching: You've already done something real here — you found three specific moments from the novel and arranged them in order, which shows you're reading closely and thinking about how events connect. Today we're working on your topic sentence, which is the sentence that opens a paragraph and tells your reader what the paragraph is *arguing*, not just what happens in it. A topic sentence is the governing claim of the paragraph — writers use it to announce the one idea that all the other sentences are working to support, so the reader always knows what the evidence is supposed to prove. In an essay, the thesis makes the central claim for the whole piece, and each topic sentence makes a smaller claim for its own paragraph, carrying the thesis forward one idea at a time. One strategy writers use is to look at all the evidence they've gathered and ask, "What do these moments add up to?" — because the answer to that question is usually the claim the paragraph is trying to make. So in one sentence, what do you think those three moments — giving away the coat, sharing the food, staying behind — are showing about the main character? Once you have that claim, we'll use it to build your topic sentence.

name: Effective topic sentence
object_raw: Supporting Detail (textual evidence from the poem)
bottleneck: claim exists; no textual detail is present. the paragraph cannot develop analytically without a specific moment from the poem.
diagnosed: no textual evidence present — highest leverage gap
no explanation/analysis connecting evidence to claim — dependent on evidence existing first
no closure/synthesis sentence — dependent on development existing first
evidence: claim is analytically specific and well-formed for this developmental moment
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: does the paragraph have at least one specific textual detail that the claim can develop and the reader can hold onto?
next: once a specific detail is located, teach the explanation move: what does this image show about the gap between love and understanding?
coaching: Your opening sentence does something a strong topic sentence should do: it names a specific pattern in the poem — the winter cold — and connects it to a meaningful idea about the relationship between father and son, which gives your reader a clear claim to follow. Now we're working on the next structural piece that every claim depends on: supporting detail, meaning the actual textual evidence from the poem. Evidence is what gives your reader a reason to believe a claim — without it, even a compelling idea floats without ground beneath it, and your reader has nothing to hold or test. In an essay, the central claim, its supporting claims, and the evidence and explanation behind them work together as a unit, and right now your paragraph needs its concrete anchor. One strategy writers use here is to ask: what does my claim require the reader to believe, and what specific moment from the text would give them a reason to believe it? With that in mind, go back to the poem and find one place where that winter cold actually appears — a line, an image, a single word — and bring it into the paragraph. Once you've located that moment, we'll work on the next move: explaining what that image shows your reader about the distance between the father's love and the son's understanding of it.

name: Poor organization
object_raw: Overall Organization
bottleneck: ideas are ordered by occurrence, not by the reader's logical need; pro-thesis reasons and complications are interleaved with no distinction.
diagnosed: overall organization: ideas in occurrence order, no reader-driven progression
thesis: present but not governing — mixed support and complication follow without distinction
communicative purpose: position stated but undermined by unresolved counter-considerations
evidence: opening sentence states a clear position
multiple distinct considerations are present
exit: can the reader reasonably follow the intended progression of ideas? (overall organization exit criterion)
next: use the sorted groups to propose a sequence (supporting reasons first, then complications, or vice versa) that reflects the argument's logic.
coaching: You've already staked out a clear position — "later is better" — and you've gathered a real range of ideas around it, which is exactly what a developing argument needs. Today we're focusing on overall organization, which is the order that lets your reader follow your ideas from start to finish; it's the element that connects your thesis to your paragraphs and makes the whole essay feel like one continuous, logical argument rather than a collection of separate thoughts. One strategy writers use when organizing an essay is to ask themselves: what are the major jobs this essay needs to do, and what order does the reader need them in? For your essay, the key sorting question is this: look back at each of your sentences and decide — does this idea support starting school later, or does it complicate or push against that position? Try grouping your sentences into two lists: reasons FOR starting later, and problems or complications — and once you've done that sorting, we'll use those two groups to build a sequence that carries your reader through your argument in a logical order.

name: Weak transition
object_raw: Transition (relationship-first) — student must name actual relationships before they can write transitions
bottleneck: student cannot yet write transitions because the underlying relationships have not been identified; transitions require relationship-first reasoning, not just connective words.
diagnosed: no transitions / relationships between sentences unsignaled
no thesis / organizing claim
ideas not connected to a central argument
evidence: four sentences all relate to junk food tax topic — student has relevant ideas
exit: reader can understand why each sentence follows from the previous one (relationship is named and visible).
next: once student can name the relationship in plain words, express it in the text as a transition.
coaching: You've already gathered four real ideas that belong in this argument — health problems, buying behavior, kids' habits, and school funding — and that's genuine groundwork for an essay. Now let's work on transitions, which are the connections between your ideas that help a reader understand why one idea follows another. An essay is built from a few elements working together — a claim, the reasons behind it, and the way those reasons connect — and transitions are what make that connection visible, keeping your whole essay coherent and organized. Here's a strategy writers use: before you write a transition, say the relationship out loud in plain words first, because you can only express a connection once you know what it is. Pick any two of your sentences — for example, the one about health problems and the one about taxes reducing what people buy — and tell me in your own words: what is the connection between those two ideas? Does one cause the other, does one lead to the other, or do they both support the same bigger point? Once you can name that relationship in plain words, we'll put it directly into the writing as a transition.

name: Forced/unnecessary transition
object_raw: Transition — understanding that transitions express real relationships, not labels
bottleneck: student pastes connectives without first identifying the real relationship between ideas. the connectives are inaccurate and redundant because no relationship was named first.
diagnosed: stacked/mechanical transition words signal no real relationship
paragraph lacks a controlling idea/topic sentence
no causal or sequential logic expressed between ideas
draft content very sparse — ideas not yet developed enough to assess photosynthesis explanation
evidence: connectives are present but inaccurate and redundant — classic mechanical application pattern.
exit: the reader can understand why each idea follows from the previous one — relationships are explicit and accurate.
next: student names the relationship between two adjacent ideas, then expresses it in the text.
coaching: You've already done something real here: you can see that your ideas need to be connected, and you've reached for transition words to do that work — that instinct matters. Today we're working on **transitions**, specifically what they're actually for. A transition helps a reader understand how one idea connects to the next — not just that *something* is coming, but *why* it follows. Right now, stacking "furthermore, moreover, in addition" together, or "consequently, therefore" together, means the words are labeling a connection without actually showing one; a strong transition grows out of a real relationship between two ideas. One strategy writers use is to state that relationship in plain words first — before choosing any transition word at all — and then let that relationship shape the wording. So pick one shift in your draft, like the move from "leaves are green" to "plants also need water," and tell me in ordinary language: what is the actual connection between those two ideas? Once you can name it, we'll work on expressing it in the writing itself, and that's what will make your whole essay hold together as a reader moves from one idea to the next.

name: Introduction with no context
object_raw: Background/Context — specifically, naming the subject and supplying minimum orienting context for a naive reader
bottleneck: student assumes the reader shares their knowledge of the subject; the introduction provides no context a naive reader could use.
diagnosed: missing subject identification — 'it' never names the printing press
no background context for naive reader
significance asserted ('huge deal') without grounding
no thesis/controlling idea about what significance means
evidence: 'it changed everything' signals awareness of historical significance
'faster and cheaper' hints at knowledge of printing/book production
exit: can the reader understand the subject and receive minimal orienting context needed to follow the explanation?
next: once the subject is named and minimal context is present, develop the controlling idea (what kind of significance will the essay explain).
coaching: You clearly feel the weight of what you're writing about — the energy in "it changed everything" and "a huge deal" tells me you already have a strong sense that this subject matters enormously, and that conviction is exactly what a good explanation needs at its core. An essay like this one is built from a few elements working together: background context, a controlling idea, and the explanation and evidence that support it — and today we're focusing on the very first of those, background/context, specifically naming your subject and giving a reader just enough orienting information to follow what comes next. Background context is what a writer provides at the opening so that a reader who knows nothing about the topic can immediately understand what they're reading about and why it's worth their attention. One strategy writers use is to ask: "What is the single most essential fact a complete newcomer would need before anything else I say could make sense?" — and then lead with exactly that, nothing more. So try this: think about a reader who has never heard of the printing press, and ask yourself what one thing they would need to know about it first in order to understand why it changed everything — then write that in your own words. Once your subject is named and that minimum context is in place, we'll move on to developing your controlling idea, which is where you tell your reader what kind of significance your essay is actually going to explain.

name: Effective introduction
object_raw: First body paragraph — articulating the supporting claim (topic sentence)
bottleneck: no body paragraph exists; the thesis is stated but not yet developed.
diagnosed: consolidate intro as sufficient and release
scaffold first body paragraph's supporting claim
thesis could eventually be tested against body development

hook is topically integrated not decorative

connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose

next: draft first body paragraph with a focused supporting claim.
coaching: Your introduction is already doing substantial work: the floor/net distinction lands as a precise, arguable thesis that gives readers a clear direction to follow, and the automation question you open with earns the stakes behind it. That's a fully functional opening, so we're ready to move forward to your first body paragraph — specifically, the supporting claim, or topic sentence, that opens it. An essay is built from a few structural elements working together: a central claim, the supporting claims that carry its weight, the evidence behind those, and the explanations that connect everything — and a strong topic sentence is where each supporting claim announces itself to the reader, giving them grounds to follow you further. One transferable strategy writers use here is to ask: what does my thesis actually require the reader to believe first, and what single reason would give them the strongest grounds to believe it? Try applying that to your own argument right now — what is the one most important reason a floor, rather than a net, is what a post-automation economy requires? Write that reason in one sentence, as specifically as you can, and once you have it, we'll build out the evidence and explanation that make the reader genuinely take it seriously.

name: Conclusion that merely repeats
object_raw: Conclusion — specifically the distinction between restatement and synthesis/significance
bottleneck: student treats restatement as completion; has not yet differentiated 'saying it again' from 'showing what it now means.'
diagnosed: conclusion is summary-only — no synthesis or significance
thesis restated twice — formulaic, no development
communicative purpose of conclusion not yet understood by student
evidence: thesis restated twice — clear summary_only pattern
phrase 'as i said/stated earlier' confirms backward-looking restatement orientation
exit: can the reader understand what the essay completed and why it matters — not just that the essay stopped?
next: student states a significance sentence, then revises the conclusion to incorporate it.

Once your thesis states that controlling idea clearly, it will guide every paragraph you write and help your reader follow your comparison from start to finish — and after that, we'll use it to decide how to organize your comparison and what to use as your basis for comparing the two approaches.

name: Cause/effect — correlation asserted as cause
object_raw: Causal mechanism — distinguishing correlation from causation and supplying the connecting process.
bottleneck: causation is asserted from co-occurrence alone; the mechanism (the process by which smartphones produce anxiety) is entirely missing.
diagnosed: correlation-as-causation: co-occurrence treated as causal proof — no mechanism supplied.
central claim is too absolute ('clearly the cause') — overstates certainty given only co-occurrence.
no consideration of alternative or contributing causes.
evidence: student correctly identifies a genuine social trend and a plausible causal candidate.
exit: can the reader understand the intended relationship between smartphones and anxiety — not just that they co-occurred, but by what process one produces the other?
next: once the student articulates a mechanism, return to the central claim and consider qualifying it and acknowledging alternative causes.
coaching: You've made a sharp observation — you noticed that teen anxiety and smartphone adoption rose at the same time, and that kind of pattern is exactly what a writer looks for when building a causal argument. Today we're working on causal mechanism, the part of your essay that explains the *process* connecting your evidence to your claim — this is the "how and why" that turns a shared timeline into an actual explanation. An essay is built from a claim, the evidence behind it, and the explanation that connects them, and causal mechanism lives in that third part: it makes explicit what your evidence means and how it actually establishes your claim, rather than leaving the reader to assume the connection. One strategy writers use here is to ask two questions in sequence: *What does this evidence show?* and then *How does that establish my claim?* — working through the reasoning one step at a time so the logic becomes visible on the page. Right now your sentence moves straight from "they rose at the same time" to "smartphones are clearly the cause," and a reader could reasonably ask whether something else might explain both trends rising together. So try this: in your own words, describe what you think actually happens between a teen picking up a phone and feeling more anxious — what is the step-by-step process? Once you've worked out that mechanism, we'll come back to your central claim and look at how to qualify it and acknowledge other possible causes.

name: Literary analysis — plot summary instead of a claim
object_raw: Thesis — move from topic/summary to an interpretive claim about theme
bottleneck: draft is a topic/summary (what happens) not a claim (what the author establishes about a theme); the student has not yet performed the retelling-to-interpretation move.
diagnosed: no thesis or interpretive claim present — draft is pure retelling
no theme identified; no authorial intent named
closing sentence ('the author shows a lot of things happening') is vague rather than analytical
evidence: closing sentence shows student is reaching toward author-awareness
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around a reasonably clear interpretive claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: use the identified theme to draft a thesis claim about how the author develops it.
coaching: You've done something real here — you've tracked the shape of the whole story, from the boy finding the bird all the way through to his sadness at the end, and that arc is exactly the raw material an analysis needs. Now let's work on your thesis, which is the one idea your whole essay exists to establish — it's the first structural piece a reader needs, and everything else in your essay (your examples, your explanation) will exist to support it. A thesis isn't a summary of what happens; it's a statement of what the author is trying to show the reader about life, people, or the world. One strategy writers use to build a thesis is to ask themselves: "What is the most important idea I want my reader to understand by the end?" — and then turn that answer into a single, focused claim. So here's your question: What do you think the story is really about — what idea or feeling does the boy's experience with the bird leave a reader with? Once you can say that in your own words, we'll use it to shape a thesis that gives your whole essay a clear direction to build around.

name: Rhetorical analysis — describes what, not how
object_raw: Thesis — specifically, converting content summary into a claim about persuasive strategy
bottleneck: draft answers 'what does the speaker say?' not 'how does he persuade?' — the thesis type required by this assignment is absent.
diagnosed: no thesis — draft summarizes content instead of claiming a rhetorical strategy
no introduction-level orientation to the analytical task
what/how confusion: student conflates content summary with rhetorical analysis
evidence: all three sentences report speaker's content/belief, consistent with summary mode
exit: can the remainder of the essay be organized around a reasonably clear analytical claim about persuasive strategy?
next: once what/how distinction is grasped, draft a thesis claiming something about the speaker's persuasive strategy.
coaching: You've done something useful already — you've tracked the speaker's core message clearly, and that shows you were listening closely to what he was saying about climate change and urgency. Now let's use that as a launching pad for the most important structural piece of this essay: your thesis, which is the single main idea your whole essay exists to establish and prove. An essay is built from a few elements that work together — your thesis sits at the center of all of them, giving your reader the one controlling idea that your introduction announces and every paragraph develops. Here's the key distinction for this assignment, though: right now your draft tells us *what* the speaker says, but a rhetorical analysis asks you to claim something about *how* he persuades — the strategies and moves he uses on his audience, not the content of his message. One strategy writers use when building a thesis like this is to ask themselves, "What is the single most important thing I want my reader to understand or accept?" — and then shape the answer into one focused, arguable statement. So try this: in one sentence, what do you think is the most important thing a reader should understand about *how* this speaker works on his audience? Once you've made that claim about strategy, we'll build your full thesis around it.

name: Research synthesis — source dump, no synthesis
object_raw: Thesis (controlling idea) — dependency: the writer's own synthesizing point must exist before any other structure can be developed
bottleneck: sources are present but no writer's claim governs them — the draft reports rather than argues or analyzes. the student needs to move from source-lister to point-maker.
diagnosed: no controlling thesis — highest-leverage gap
sources not integrated into writer's reasoning — synthesis absent
no explanation/interpretation connecting evidence to any claim
evidence: three sources are cited — student has done research and can attribute views
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around a reasonably clear controlling claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: once the student articulates their own point, shape it into a focused, contestable thesis and then move to synthesis (how the sources support it together).
coaching: You've already done something real researchers do: you went out and found multiple sources that don't all say the same thing, and you laid them honestly side by side. Now let's work on your thesis — the single main idea your whole essay exists to establish for your reader. A thesis isn't just a topic or a list of what sources say; it's the one claim you want your reader to walk away understanding or accepting, and everything else in your essay exists to build toward it. One strategy writers use here is to ask themselves: "If my reader forgets all the details, what is the one most important thing I want them to believe or understand?" — and then turn that answer into a focused, supportable statement. In an essay, that thesis sits at the heart of your introduction and gives your organization, your evidence, and your whole purpose a direction to move in. Before we can sharpen the thesis itself, we need the idea underneath it — your own judgment about what these three sources, taken together, are actually showing. Try finishing this sentence in your own words: *When you look at what these sources show together, the most important thing to understand about remote learning is…* Once you have that idea down, we'll shape it into a focused thesis and then look at how your sources work together to support it.

name: Lab report — subjective register in methods
object_raw: Register and word choice — shift from personal narrative to objective, precise procedural language
bottleneck: student is using a personal-narrative register where a replication-enabling procedural register is required; word choice is evaluative and vague rather than precise and measurable.
diagnosed: register: informal/personal tone incompatible with scientific methods writing
word choice: vague ('a lot,' 'a while,' 'pretty fun') — no measurable specifics
paragraph purpose: narrative purpose substituting for procedural purpose
supporting detail: no concrete procedural steps
evidence: 'pretty fun,' 'kind of,' 'a lot,' 'a while' all confirm informal personal register
exit: tone: student sets an appropriate, consistent objective stance suited to a scientific methods reader (no personal evaluation; language is measurable and specific enough to support replication).
next: once one sentence is rewritten in objective register, extend to full procedural sequence with specific measurable details.
coaching: You've already captured the core sequence of your experiment — heating water and observing a result — and that underlying structure is exactly what a methods section needs to convey. A lab report is built from a few key elements working together: the methods section is the part where you tell a reader precisely *what was done*, so they could walk into a lab and repeat your experiment step by step. That's actually the key to today's work — we're focusing on **register and word choice**, which means shifting from personal narrative into objective, precise procedural language. Register is the tone and word choice a writer chooses to match their audience; in a methods section, your reader isn't there to hear how the experience felt — they're there to *replicate* what you did, so every word needs to describe an action, not a reaction. One strategy writers use when making this shift is to ask of each sentence: *does this describe what was done, or does it describe how I felt about it?* — then replace any feeling or judgment words with measurable, observable ones (so "a lot" becomes a temperature, and "pretty fun" disappears entirely). Try rewriting just your first sentence — remove any personal reaction and describe only the action that took place, as if you're writing instructions for someone who wasn't there. Once you have one sentence in that objective voice, we'll build outward into a full procedural sequence with specific, measurable details throughout.

name: Persuasive letter — audience/tone mismatch
object_raw: Audience awareness — modeling the principal as a specific reader requiring respectful, formal address and a concrete proposal
bottleneck: student writes only from personal feeling without modeling the principal as a formal authority reader who needs a respectful, specific ask.
diagnosed: tone severely mismatched to principal audience (casual/accusatory vs. formal/respectful)
no specific proposal named — communicative purpose undefined
no audience modeling — writes only from personal frustration
no structure — single sentence, no letter conventions
evidence: draft expresses genuine concern — motivational basis for engagement
exit: student can identify the principal as a specific reader with distinct needs and produce a respectful, concrete opening ask.
next: once a specific proposal and respectful framing are in place, develop tone consistency and supporting reasons.
coaching: You've identified something real here — there's a genuine frustration driving this letter, and that kind of conviction is exactly what makes a proposal worth reading. Today we're working on **audience awareness**, which means thinking carefully about who your specific reader is and what they need from you in order to act. A letter to a principal is built from a few moving parts — a clear proposal, reasons that support it, and a tone that fits the relationship — and audience awareness is what holds all of those together, because every choice you make (how you open, what you ask for, how you say it) has to work for that particular reader. A principal is a formal reader with real authority, which means they'll respond to a respectful, specific request far more than to a complaint — and one strategy writers use is to picture that reader holding the letter and ask: *what does this person need to know, and how do they need to be addressed, before they'll take this seriously?* So here's your first move: picture your principal reading your words — what is the **one specific change** you're actually proposing (new menu options? a different vendor? more choices?), and how would you phrase that ask so your reader feels respected rather than accused? Once you have a clear, courteous proposal in your own words, we'll come back to building out the full audience-aware framing — and after that, we'll develop the reasons and evidence that make your case impossible to ignore.

name: Op-ed — strong public-audience opening (restraint)
object_raw: Central Claim — elicit the student's position before drafting proceeds
bottleneck: hook is complete and effective; no central claim has been articulated — continuation risks drifting without a governing position.
diagnosed: consolidate and name the hook's effectiveness (it meets exit criterion)
identify/develop the central claim — the position the op-ed will argue
background/context for the general reader (what bridge? what decision-makers?)
evidence: concrete scene with specific numbers ('two thousand commuters', 'a decade ago') signals audience awareness
pivot sentence ('it is not… it is') shows rhetorical intentionality
strategy: brief consolidation of what the student has learned
connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: hook: does the opening give the reader a genuine, relevant reason to care connected to the essay's purpose? yes — met.
next: articulate the central claim, then begin drafting the body in service of it.
coaching: Your opening does something a newspaper op-ed really needs: that image of two thousand commuters idling on an unsafe bridge puts a reader immediately inside the problem, and your reframe — "it is not a budget problem; it is a decision" — signals that you have a sharp, arguable position forming. Now, before you draft the next paragraph, the structural element to get clear is your central claim, sometimes called a thesis — the single main idea your whole essay exists to establish and make a reader accept. In an op-ed, that claim is the engine everything else runs on: your introduction earns attention, but the claim tells your reader exactly what position they're being asked to take seriously. One strategy writers use here is to ask themselves, "What is the most important thing I want my reader to believe or do by the end of this piece?" — and then turn the honest answer to that question into one focused, supportable statement. So before you write another sentence: in your own words, what is that position? Once you can state it plainly, you'll have the anchor that every paragraph in the body can be built around.

name: Personal statement — cliché instead of authentic voice
object_raw: Voice / Opening Move — surface the specific, owned moment before drafting
bottleneck: no specific experiential material — writing is generic declaration, not owned reflection; the dependency (a concrete moment) does not yet exist.
diagnosed: opening is generic/clichéd — no specific moment or owned detail
voice is absent — writing sounds borrowed, not the student's own
formative experience not yet identified or named specifically
no hook that creates relevant reader interest
evidence: two distinct themes suggest the student has real experiences to draw from
exit: can the opening give a reader a genuine reason to care and signal the real subject of this particular writer's essay?
next: once a specific moment is identified, develop it as the opening move and connect it to the essay's reflective purpose.
coaching: You already know the two things that shaped you — a drive to help people and the lessons sports gave you — and naming them shows you have a real subject to write about. Today we're working on your opening move, which is the part of a personal statement that brings a reader into your world before anything else. An introduction's job is to prepare your reader for what your essay will be about and why it matters — and in a college essay, it does that by making the reader feel they are somewhere specific, with *you*, rather than reading a phrase they've encountered a hundred times before. The opening move works alongside your thesis, your background context, and your sense of purpose — all the structural elements that together tell a reader who you are and why this story is worth following. A strategy writers use here is to ask: what does my reader need to *feel or see* before I can tell them what I believe? — what single moment would make this problem real for them? So before you draft anything new, try this: think of one specific scene from your experience — a single instant, image, or exchange that you keep returning to — and just describe it to me in a few sentences, without explaining what it means yet. Once you have that moment on the page, we'll build it into the opening that pulls your reader straight into your story.

name: Business email — buries the purpose
object_raw: Communicative Purpose — articulate the specific request the email exists to make
bottleneck: the email's only communicative job — a specific, time-bounded request — is entirely absent from the current draft.
diagnosed: communicative purpose absent — no request, deadline, or document named
audience awareness weak — colleague cannot identify what is being asked
tone/register: overly casual social opener may not suit professional request context
evidence: social opener shows awareness of audience relationship
exit: can the remainder of the email be organized around a reasonably clear communicative purpose (the specific request)?
next: once request is stated, develop audience context (what does the colleague need to know to act?)
coaching: Your warm, conversational opening does something real — it signals goodwill and sets a collegial tone, which genuinely matters in professional writing. Today we're working on communicative purpose, the structural element that tells your reader exactly what you need them to do by the time they finish reading. In any professional email, your purpose is what you want your reader to understand or believe — and here, that means a specific request and a deadline. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves, "What should be *different* for the reader after reading this?" — and then use that answer to test whether the current draft actually delivers it. Right now a colleague reading your opening would know you're friendly, but not that a review request with a Friday deadline is coming; that request is the core everything else — your tone, your details, your closing — needs to organize around. Try completing this sentence in your own words: "I'm writing to ask you to _______ by _______." Once that request is clearly in place, we'll turn to audience context — what your colleague needs to know in order to actually act on it.

name: Cover letter — claims without evidence
object_raw: Evidence — concrete support for at least one qualification claim
bottleneck: student has claims but no concrete supporting instances — the paragraph cannot persuade a skeptical reader without them.
diagnosed: evidence entirely absent — claims unsupported
claims are generic/absolute (no qualification/scope)
no specific example or detail present
evidence: student has identified three distinct, relevant qualities.
exit: can the claim now be reasonably accepted or considered by the reader? (evidence exit: the claim is substantially earned for the intended reader.)
next: once one concrete instance is named, connect it explicitly to the claim it supports (explanation).
coaching: You've given your reader a clear picture of how you see yourself — hard worker, team player, detail-oriented — and that confident self-presentation is a real starting point for a strong cover letter. Now let's work on **evidence**, the structural element that gives your reader actual reasons to believe those claims. Evidence works by showing a specific instance — something you did, a result you produced, or a situation you navigated — and it's what moves a claim from assertion to something a reader can genuinely consider and trust. A strategy writers use here is to ask: *what would a reader need to see or know in order to believe this quality is real?* Pick just one of your three qualities — whichever one you have the clearest memory around — and think of a real moment from your experience that demonstrates it: what happened, what you did, what came of it. Once you have that concrete instance on the page, we'll work on connecting it explicitly back to the claim it supports — that connection is called explanation, and it's the next move we'll make together.

name: Summary/precis — inserts opinion, loses fidelity
object_raw: Communicative purpose of summary — objectivity, withhold opinion
bottleneck: student is treating summary as an opportunity to share opinion; the purpose of a summary is to report, not evaluate.
diagnosed: opinion sentence violates objectivity requirement — core purpose failure
no stated main idea of the article (controlling summary claim absent)
hedged language ('i guess') also signals opinion leakage into tone
vague opening ('the article talks about zoos') does not summarize a main argument

coaching: You've already pulled out something real from the article — the detail about zoos helping endangered animals shows you're reading for content, which is exactly what a summary writer needs to do. Today we're working on the communicative purpose of a summary, which is the writing element that shapes every other choice you'll make: your tone, your organization, and the way your reader experiences the whole piece. A summary's purpose is to leave the reader understanding what the *source* says — not what *you* think about it — so every sentence should move the reader closer to the article's ideas, not your own opinion. One strategy writers use to stay on track with this purpose is to pause and ask, "After reading this, what will my reader understand about the article?" — then check whether each sentence actually serves that goal. When you look at your draft with that question in mind, you'll notice a sentence that shares your personal view, and a summary is the one kind of writing where that move works against your purpose. Try this: in one sentence, tell me what the article is mainly saying, using only what it reports — no "I think" or "if you ask me." Once you can state the article's main idea that way, we'll use that sentence to build a strong, objective opening for your whole summary.

name: Annotated bibliography — describes, doesn't evaluate
object_raw: Communicative purpose of the annotation — clarify what the annotation should accomplish for a reader
bottleneck: student equates annotation with description; the evaluative communicative purpose (help a reader judge the source) is absent.
diagnosed: no evaluative claim or central assertion present — only description
communicative purpose of annotation genre not yet grasped
no connection to research project purpose or research question
no reasoning about credibility, relevance, or reliability

exit: can the student state what the annotation is trying to accomplish for a reader (evaluate trustworthiness/relevance), distinct from merely describing the source?

coaching: You've already done something useful here — you've gathered the basic facts about your source: its topic, its author, its date, and its length. That's a real starting point. Now let's focus on the **communicative purpose of your annotation** — what this piece of writing is actually supposed to do for a reader. An annotation's purpose is what you want your reader to understand or believe by the end: not just *what* the source is, but *whether it's worth using and why*. One strategy writers use is to ask, "What should be different for my reader after they finish reading this?" — and then check whether every sentence in the draft is working toward that change. Right now your sentences describe the source, but an annotation coordinates its details, judgments, and evidence toward one goal: helping a reader decide whether to trust and use the source. So try this: in one sentence, what's the single most important thing a reader would need to know about this source to judge whether it's reliable or useful for their research? Once you've named that, we'll use it to build a central evaluative claim.

name: Creative/poetry — do not impose essay logic
object_raw: Voice / communicative purpose: what the speaker's pretending conceals — the emotional core that will govern further drafting
bottleneck: the images are doing real work, but the writer has not yet named (even to themselves) what emotional stake the pretending holds — so they cannot yet make deliberate choices about what to add or withhold.
diagnosed: developing the speaker's emotional stance (what is being suppressed or avoided) to guide further drafting
voice — a distinct presence is emerging through compression and indirection; could be named and consolidated
tone — the compressed, nighttime intimacy is present but not yet consciously controlled
line-break and image selection as the poem expands

sensory specificity (the moth, the cough) suggests deliberate selection
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: the writer can name (even privately) what emotional experience the poem is circling — sufficient for purposeful continuation of the draft.

coaching: The way you've built these four lines — porch light, moth, cough, then that final quiet act of pretending — creates a scene that feels genuinely held-breath and tense, and "I pretend to be asleep" lands with real weight because of everything placed before it. A poem, like any piece of writing, is built from a few elements working together: the images you choose, the voice speaking them, the tone, and underneath all of those, a communicative purpose — what you want your reader to understand or feel differently by the end. That's the element we're working on right now: the emotional core the speaker's pretending conceals, because that interior is what will govern every choice you make as you draft further. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves, "What should become different for the reader after reading this?" — and then check whether the current lines are actually moving toward that change. Right now your images are accumulating with real power, but the speaker's relationship to the moth and the cough and the porch light is still slightly hidden, even from the writer. So before you draft another line, just tell me in plain words: what is the speaker pretending not to know, or not to feel, in that moment? Once we name that, we'll come back to the poem and let it guide every image and line from here.

name: Reflective portfolio — stops at events, no significance
object_raw: Communicative Purpose — student must articulate what they want the reader to understand before any other structure can be built
bottleneck: student equates the task with reporting what happened; the reflective purpose (what it meant / what was learned) is entirely absent.
diagnosed: communicative purpose absent — draft recounts events, no reflective intent stated
controlling insight / thesis absent — no meaning-claim exists yet
explanation absent — no interpretation of what events meant

exit: can the remainder of the composition be organized around a reasonably clear communicative purpose?
next: once purpose is articulated, use it to develop a controlling insight / thesis-equivalent for the reflection.
coaching: You've laid out exactly what happened during your project — picking a topic, researching, presenting, earning that grade — and that clear sense of sequence shows you can organize your experience, which is a real foundation to build on. Today we're working on something called **communicative purpose**, the element that drives every other decision a writer makes. Your purpose is what you want your reader to understand or believe by the end — it's the reason you're writing at all, and once it's clear, it shapes your thesis, your organization, your tone, everything. A strategy writers use is to ask themselves: *What should be different for my reader after finishing this?* — and then check whether the writing is actually aimed at that change. Right now your draft tells us what occurred, but a reflection's real job is to share what the experience *meant* to you, not just the order it happened in. So here's the one move I'd like you to try: in a single sentence, complete this thought — *"By the end of this reflection, I want my reader to understand that I learned _____."* Once you have that answer, we'll use it to build the controlling insight at the heart of your reflection.

name: Audience awareness — too technical for lay reader
object_raw: Audience Awareness — modeling a non-expert reader before drafting further
bottleneck: student is writing writer-only — no evidence of modeling a non-expert reader; every word choice assumes expert knowledge the assignment's audience lacks.
diagnosed: no audience modeling — sentence assumes expert reader; dense technical vocabulary inaccessible to general audience

coaching: Your sentence shows you have precise command of your methodology — you know exactly what you did and how to name it with technical accuracy, and that precision is real expertise. Now, before drafting further, let's work on audience awareness: the practice of modeling who your reader is and what they already know before deciding how to say anything. Writers use this because every word choice, every term, every level of assumed knowledge either opens a door for a reader or closes it — and a general audience needs different doors than your research community does. In an explanatory piece for non-experts, audience awareness isn't decorative; it's the foundation that holds everything else together, because your claim, your background, and your evidence can only land if the reader has footholds in your language. One strategy writers use is to picture a single specific reader — someone intelligent but entirely outside your field — and ask what that person would need to know *first*, before any process or method makes sense to them. Once you can answer that, we'll build on it to develop the orienting background that lets a non-expert reader follow everything that comes after.

name: Tone inconsistency — casual in a formal task
object_raw: Register (Tone/Word Choice consistency)
bottleneck: the student can initiate formal register but does not yet sustain it; the colloquial turn undermines the analytical relationship with the reader.
diagnosed: register inconsistency: sentence 2 is casual/colloquial against a formal assignment
no controlling thesis yet present
