coaching: Your opening sentence — "Economic inequality is a serious structural problem" — does something real: it establishes a formal, analytical voice that signals to your reader that you're writing with purpose and credibility. Today we're working on **register**, which is the level of formality your word choices create throughout a piece of writing, and keeping it consistent is one of the things that makes an essay feel authoritative rather than accidental. An essay is built from a few elements working together — a claim, the reasoning and evidence behind it, and the language that holds all of it in place for your intended audience — and register is what governs the language layer across every sentence. One strategy writers use to maintain consistent register is to read each sentence and ask: *does this word choice belong in the same room as my most formal sentence?* — if it doesn't, they rephrase the idea without changing what they mean. Your second sentence actually carries a real idea worth keeping, but words like "kinda," "lol," and "super messed up" shift the register away from the formal stance your first sentence sets up, so the work right now is yours: can you restate that same idea from your second sentence in language that matches the analytical voice of your first? Once your register feels consistent throughout, we'll move into building a controlling thesis — the sentence that tells your reader exactly what your whole essay will argue.

name: Vague diction — 'things' and 'stuff'
object_raw: Word choice within the thesis — replace vague placeholders with specific language
bottleneck: student has an idea but has not yet translated it into language that carries meaning — 'stuff,' 'things,' 'better' are stand-ins for a real claim.
diagnosed: thesis is present but vague — placeholder words prevent any real claim
word choice: 'stuff,' 'things,' 'better' carry no specific meaning
no introduction or body yet drafted
evidence: sentence attempts a thesis shape — topic + value judgment + reason
exit: can the remainder of the composition be organized around a reasonably clear communicative purpose? — not yet; no specific claim exists.
next: once a specific benefit is named, use it to make the thesis claim precise and supportable.
coaching: You've already done something important: you've identified your subject and taken a clear position that playing music matters to you — that's the foundation a thesis needs. A thesis is the one sentence that tells your reader the main idea your whole essay is trying to establish, and it sits at the heart of everything else — your introduction, your organization, every paragraph you write all exist to back it up. Right now, though, words like "stuff," "things," and "better" are holding your thesis back, because they don't yet tell a reader *what* music actually does for you. One move writers use when sharpening a thesis is to ask: "What is the single most important idea I want my reader to understand?" — and then say that idea in plain, specific language instead of a placeholder. So try this: pick just *one* specific thing playing music does for you and name it directly — what exactly does it help with, in your own words? Once you've named that one specific benefit, we'll bring it back into your thesis and make your central claim precise enough that a reader could restate it after a single reading.

name: Sentence variety — choppy monotony
object_raw: Sentence variety — using longer setup sentences to make short punch sentences land harder at key moments
bottleneck: uniform sentence structure flattens all moments equally — no sentence carries emphasis, so the narrative lacks rhythm and emotional arc.
diagnosed: all sentences identical in length/structure — no rhythmic contrast, no emphasis
key emotional moments (missing bus, arriving late) carry no more weight than filler actions
no use of subordination, coordination, or varied syntax to build tension
evidence: eight syntactically identical sentences confirm the pattern is consistent, not accidental
exit: at least one instance of deliberate contrast between a longer setup sentence and a short emphatic sentence at a key narrative moment.
next: student combines or expands sentences around a key moment; then consolidate the rhythm-emphasis principle.
coaching: Your story moves — you've captured the full rush of a bad morning in a tight sequence that pulls the reader straight through from alarm to late arrival. Today we're working on sentence variety, specifically the way writers use longer setup sentences to make short, punchy sentences hit harder at key moments. A narrative paragraph is built from a few working parts — the events, the details, and the rhythm that tells a reader what to notice — and sentence variety is what controls that rhythm. Here's the transferable move: a short sentence packs its biggest punch when a longer one has already built up some tension just before it; without that contrast, every sentence feels the same weight, and the big moments get lost. Right now each sentence follows the same "I did X" pattern, which flattens the whole rush into one even pace — so look at your two most important moments, missing the bus and arriving late. Which of the sentences just before those could you combine or expand, stretching the tension a little, so the short sentence that follows lands like a door slamming? Once you've created even one of those setups, we'll look at how you might combine or expand sentences around other key moments to lock in that rhythm throughout the paragraph.

name: Cohesion — paragraphs don't connect
object_raw: Thesis — establish a single controlling claim the essay will argue
bottleneck: draft contains observations (topic-level) but no contestable position — thesis is missing entirely.
diagnosed: no thesis / controlling claim present
sentences read as disconnected facts, not as support for a position
no paragraph structure; no topic sentences
evidence: assignment clearly calls for argumentation; student has produced factual material that could serve as support
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around a reasonably clear central claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: once a thesis claim is formulated, align the four sentences as potential supporting points and introduce paragraph purpose.
coaching: You've already gathered some real, specific details about libraries — internet access, community events, funding cuts — and those are exactly the kinds of facts that can power a strong argument. An essay like this one is built from a few elements that work together: a central claim, the reasons and evidence behind it, and the way everything connects — so today we're focusing on your thesis, the single sentence that tells your reader the main idea your whole essay exists to establish and develop. A thesis isn't just a topic; it's a position — the one thing you want a thoughtful reader to understand or accept by the end. One strategy writers use is to ask themselves, "What is the most important idea I want my reader to walk away believing?" — and then turn that answer into a focused, arguable statement, not a list of facts. Looking at what you've already written, try this: in one sentence, what is the most important thing you want your reader to believe about public libraries after finishing your essay? Once that claim is clear, we'll come back to your four sentences and look at how each one can work as a supporting point for it.

name: Counterargument absent in an argument
object_raw: Counterargument — identify and articulate the strongest opposing view
bottleneck: no counterargument present; likely misconception that stating obvious benefits is sufficient — opposing views ignored.
diagnosed: thesis is contestable and on-assignment but reasons are bare assertions needing development
no counterargument present — governing pedagogical purpose is explicitly to develop this
second sentence ('these are all clearly good things') asserts rather than earns agreement
evidence: thesis is contestable and directly answers the assignment
exit: counterargument: a genuine, fairly-stated opposing view is present and its reasoning is shown.
next: once a genuine counterargument is articulated, develop a rebuttal/response.
coaching: Your opening move is genuinely strong — you've staked out a clear position and backed it with three distinct reasons, which means your thesis is already doing real work for your reader. An essay like this is built from a few elements working together: your claim, the reasons behind it, and — crucially — an honest reckoning with the opposing view, which is what we're focusing on today. A **counterargument** is the part of a persuasive essay where you fairly represent the strongest case *against* your position; writers include it not to weaken their argument, but to show they've thought seriously about the full picture, which actually makes readers trust the argument more. One strategy writers use when building a counterargument is to imagine the most reasonable, thoughtful person who disagrees with them — not someone being stubborn, but someone with a genuine concern — and then articulate *their* best reason, not just a weak version of it. So here's your writing move: look at your claim that cars should be banned downtown, and ask yourself what a reasonable person on the other side would say is the strongest single reason to keep cars there — then write that reason out in a sentence or two, in their voice, making their case as fairly as you can. Once you've got a genuine opposing view on the page, we'll move to the next step: building your rebuttal, where you respond to that objection directly.

name: Concession is a straw man
object_raw: Counterargument — replace straw man with a genuine opposing reason
bottleneck: straw man — opposing side is caricatured as morally deficient rather than given a real, reasonable argument.
diagnosed: straw man counterargument — opposing side caricatured as uncaring
no central claim / thesis present
no reasoning given for the opposing view
evidence: student attempted to represent the other side — shows some rhetorical awareness
exit: a meaningful alternative perspective is identified and represented fairly (not caricatured).
next: state a genuine opposing reason; then develop the rebuttal.
coaching: You've already done something real here — you've recognized that people disagree about the four-day school week and decided to take that disagreement on directly, which is exactly what a strong persuasive essay needs. Today we're working on your counterargument, the part of an essay where you represent the other side before you push back against it. A counterargument works best when it gives the opposing view its strongest, most honest form — that way, when you respond to it, your reader sees you as fair and your argument comes across as more convincing. Right now your sentence says opponents "don't care about students," but that move is called a straw man: it shrinks the other side down to a weak version that's easy to knock over, and careful readers notice. One strategy writers use is to ask, "What would a thoughtful, reasonable person on the other side actually say?" — not what motive you might guess at, but a real concern they could argue with facts or logic. So here's your move: what is one genuine worry — something a reasonable person could honestly believe — that someone against a four-day school week might bring up? Once you've named that real concern, we'll come back and build the full counterargument: stating their reason fairly, then crafting your rebuttal.

name: Conclusion introduces a new argument
object_raw: Conclusion function: completing vs. opening new argument
bottleneck: student introduces a new unsupported claim rather than completing the essay's existing reasoning — the conclusion function is not yet understood as completion vs. new argument.
diagnosed: new unsupported claim (nuclear power) introduced — conclusion fracture; highest priority
vague restatement without synthesis or significance
no 'so what' — significance entirely absent
evidence: 'in conclusion' signals student knows conclusions exist as a section
nuclear power sentence is clearly a new argument, not closure
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: can the reader understand that this unit of writing has reached a natural stopping point that completes the essay's communicative purpose?
next: student identifies what the body essay established, enabling synthesis and 'so what.'
coaching: Your instinct to signal a closing — "renewable energy is important" — shows you already sense that a conclusion needs to land somewhere, and that's a real writer's move. Today we're focusing on conclusion function: specifically, the difference between completing an argument and opening a new one. A conclusion's job is to give your reader the feeling that the essay has arrived at a resting point — not that a fresh journey is beginning, which is what happens when you introduce the nuclear power claim in that final sentence. An essay is built from a thesis, the reasons and evidence behind it, and a conclusion that closes the loop on all of that by clarifying what was established and why it matters. One strategy writers use here is to ask: *What can my reader now understand that wasn't clear at the start — and why does that matter?* So here's your one move: look back at the body of your essay and identify the single idea about renewable energy that you actually built and defended there — then try rewriting your conclusion so it completes *that* idea, not a new one. Once your conclusion is doing that closing work, we'll look at how to synthesize what your body established so the ending really resonates.

name: Wordiness / padding
object_raw: Word choice — identifying and removing padding/filler so the claim is stated directly
bottleneck: the sentence contains ~30 words of padding around a 4-word claim; every communicative function is blocked until the padding is cleared.
diagnosed: remove filler/padding phrases that delay the claim
sharpen the actual claim (vague: 'fitness is important')
eliminate redundant hedges ('basically very much,' 'generally tend to')
evidence: sentence is ~35 words; stripped claim is ~4 words — ratio confirms severe padding
exit: the sentence states its point directly so the reader can identify the claim without re-reading.
next: once padding is cleared, sharpen the specificity of the claim itself.
coaching: You do have a clear idea in this sentence — there's a genuine belief about fitness sitting inside it, and that's the raw material a strong argument needs. Today we're working on word choice, specifically identifying and removing padding so your claim comes through directly. Padding means words and phrases that take up space without adding meaning — phrases like "due to the fact that," "in this day and age," "basically very much," and "it can be said that" are all doing that here, wrapping your real point in extra layers before the reader can reach it. In an argument paragraph, your opening claim is the engine that drives everything else — the reasons and evidence you'll add later — so that claim needs to be clear and immediate from the first word. One strategy writers use is to ask: *what is the one thing I want my reader to believe?* — then open the sentence with exactly that, cutting every word that could be removed without losing anything. Try rewriting your sentence so it leads with your actual claim about fitness, using only the words that earn their place. Once your claim is stated directly, we'll work on sharpening it so it's as specific as possible.

name: Quote dropped in without attribution/integration
object_raw: Explanation — connect the quotation to the claim with explicit reasoning
bottleneck: third sentence restates the claim rather than interpreting the quotation — the 'because' (what the image means and why it shows loneliness) is missing.
diagnosed: missing interpretation/explanation between quotation and claim
final sentence restates claim rather than reasons from the evidence
no signal phrase / attribution for the quotation
evidence: student placed claim before quotation — shows developing sense of evidence integration order
exit: can the reader understand what the quoted image means and how it establishes the loneliness claim? (explanation exit: reader can follow the intended relationship among the ideas.)
next: once explanation is drafted, consolidate and introduce signal phrase / attribution
coaching: You've already done two important things: you've stated a clear claim ("the character is lonely") and you've chosen a quotation from the text to back it up. Now let's work on the part that connects them — **explanation**, which is the reasoning that shows your reader *how* your evidence actually supports your claim. An essay is built from a claim, evidence, and the explanation that links them together, and without that last piece, a reader can see your quote sitting next to your claim but can't follow the logic between them. One strategy writers use is to ask two questions after every quotation: *What does this show?* and *How does that help establish my claim?* — moving through those questions one step at a time builds the reasoning your reader needs. Try it with your own words: look at that image of an empty house and a phone that never rings, and in one or two sentences after the quote, tell your reader what that specific detail means and why it reveals the feeling you named. Once your explanation makes that connection clear, we'll move on to how to introduce your quotation smoothly with a signal phrase.

name: Faulty parallelism in a series
object_raw: parallel structure in coordinated series
bottleneck: the three series items use three different grammatical forms, violating the parallel-structure expectation that gives coordinated lists their clarity and rhythm.
diagnosed: parallel structure broken across three list items
sentence could become a thesis/topic sentence with further development
no elaboration yet — whole draft is one sentence
evidence: three benefits are substantively clear and relevant to the assignment
strategy: parallel example unrelated to the student's topic
exit: each item in the coordinated series uses the same grammatical form so the reader processes them as equivalent.
next: rewrite the sentence with all three items parallel; then expand toward a full opening sentence or thesis.
coaching: You've already done something important here — you've identified three genuine benefits of volunteering and pulled them together into one sentence, which is exactly the kind of move strong writers make. Now let's sharpen that sentence by working on **parallel structure in a coordinated series**, which is the element that makes a list feel balanced and clear to a reader. Parallel structure means that when you list items together, each one follows the same grammatical form — writers use it because matching forms signal to the reader that the items belong together as equals. The strategy is straightforward: look at your first item and treat it as your template, then rewrite every other item to match that same form. Right now your list mixes three different forms — "meet people," "learning new skills," and "it builds your confidence" — so can you rewrite all three so they start the same way, the way "meet people" does? Once your list is parallel, this sentence becomes a much stronger foundation for a full thesis, which is where we're headed next.

name: Point-of-view shifting (you/one/I)
object_raw: Consistent point of view (sentence-level coherence/reader orientation)
bottleneck: pov inconsistency creates an unexplained shift that prevents the reader from following whose experience is described.
diagnosed: pov inconsistency within the sentence (i/you/one/we)
paragraph governing purpose not yet established (no controlling idea)
strategies named but undeveloped
evidence: student produced a full sentence with two concrete strategies — shows engagement with the task
exit: the reader can follow the line of thought without confusion about who is being addressed.
next: once pov is consistent in this sentence, establish a controlling idea for the paragraph.
coaching: You've already identified two real strategies for managing stress — walking and breathing exercises — and that kind of concrete detail is exactly what readers find useful. As you build this essay, every sentence works as part of a larger structure: a claim, the reasons behind it, and the way those reasons connect — and today we're focusing on one element that holds all of that together at the sentence level: **consistent point of view**, which is how a writer decides who they're talking to and stays with that choice. Point of view is the voice position a writer commits to — "I," "you," or "one" — so the reader always knows who is being addressed and never has to stop and reorient. One strategy writers use is to choose their reader position before drafting a sentence and then read it back, asking: *is every pronoun still speaking to the same person?* Right now your sentence opens with "I feel stressed," shifts to "you should," then moves to "one can," and ends with "we feel" — four different positions in one breath, which makes it hard for a reader to follow. Try rewriting just that sentence in one consistent voice: either stay with "I" throughout (writing from your own experience) or stay with "you" throughout (speaking directly to your reader). Once your point of view is steady in this sentence, we'll use that same clarity to build a controlling idea for your whole paragraph.

name: Multilingual writer — surface errors, strong idea
object_raw: Thesis — clarify position + single governing reason
bottleneck: position is present and contestable; the governing reason is bundled (two reasons fused) so the thesis lacks a single clear organizing claim.
diagnosed: thesis bundles two reasons unclearly; reason structure needs sharpening
surface grammar issues (subject-verb agreement, verb form) present but not blocking
evidence: clear position stated: 'homework should not be graded'
reason present even if bundled
exit: can every part of the essay be organized around this one central claim, and could a thoughtful reader restate it?
next: once thesis states one clear position + reason, proceed to introduction framing and body planning.
coaching: You've already done something real writers do: you staked out a clear, contestable position ("homework should not be graded") and started connecting it to a reason — that's a genuine move toward an argument. Let's focus now on your thesis, which is the single sentence that tells your reader the one main idea your whole essay exists to prove. A thesis isn't just a topic or an opinion — it's the central claim your reader should be able to hold onto and expect every paragraph to develop. One strategy writers use is to pause and ask: "What is the single most important idea I want my reader to understand or accept?" — then shape the answer into one focused, supportable statement, setting aside any reasons that feel secondary. Right now your sentence carries your position and a reason, but the reason unfolds in a few connected steps that blur together a little, making it hard for a reader to pin down your one governing idea. Can you try writing it as one clear sentence — your position first, then the single most important reason behind it, in your own words? Once your thesis states one clear position and one strong reason, we'll move into shaping your introduction and planning your body paragraphs around it.

name: Student pastes AI-generated text and asks 'is this good?'
object_raw: Hook / Opening Move — developing a purpose-connected opening rather than a decorative label.
bottleneck: the opening labels the topic comprehensively but gives the reader no genuine reason to enter it; the student has not yet located what is actually compelling about urban green space for their argument.
diagnosed: opening move is decorative/inflated rather than purpose-connected — does not give a genuine reason to care.
no central claim or thesis present.
word choice is inflated ('multifaceted nexus,' 'holistically,' 'paradigms') — obscures rather than clarifies.
no background/context provided; reader has no orientation beyond a topic label.
evidence: three-category list suggests the student has some background knowledge of the topic
strategy: connection between local writing and whole-essay purpose
exit: the opening gives the reader a genuine, relevant reason to care about the subject and connects clearly to the essay's purpose.
next: student names their genuine entry point → use that to develop a thesis-level claim and then purposeful context.
coaching: Your opening sentence already shows real ambition — you've identified three distinct dimensions of urban green space (ecological, psychological, socioeconomic), which tells me you've thought seriously about how complex this topic is, and that range of thinking is exactly what a strong argument can build on. An essay is constructed from a few elements working together — a hook, a thesis, reasons, and evidence — and today we're focusing on your **hook, or opening move**: the part that gives your reader a genuine reason to care before you've made your full argument. A hook isn't a label that names all the parts of a topic; instead, it's an entry point that makes the reader feel something is unresolved, surprising, or at stake — it's what draws someone into your specific argument rather than the topic in general. One strategy writers use here is to ask: *What does this opening show my reader, and how does that lead them toward my claim?* — if the answer is "it lists categories," the hook is doing cataloguing work rather than argumentative work, and it's worth finding the sharper edge. So before we develop that opening move, I want to ask you directly: of everything you listed — the ecological, the psychological, the socioeconomic — what is the one thing about urban green space that you actually find most interesting, surprising, or urgent? Once you name that genuine entry point, we'll use it to build a thesis-level claim, and then shape an opening that earns your reader's attention by putting that real stake on the table first.

name: Perfectionist stuck — won't commit anything
object_raw: Communicative Purpose — surface any raw position/opinion to break the block
bottleneck: purpose has collapsed into 'complete the assignment correctly' — student cannot act because they have no owned position yet.
diagnosed: no draft exists; student is blocked by perfectionism
communicative purpose not yet articulated by student
no thesis or even raw position available
evidence: 'nothing i write is good enough' signals a position exists but is being suppressed
exit: can the remainder of the composition be organized around a reasonably clear communicative purpose? — no; not until the student articulates any position.
next: turn the raw sentence into a contestable thesis claim.
coaching: The fact that you keep deleting things tells me something real: you actually care whether what you write is true, and that instinct is exactly what good writers run on. Right now, let's focus on something called your communicative purpose — the part of writing where you figure out what you want your reader to understand or believe by the end, before anything else gets built. Every essay is made of a few structural elements working together — a thesis, a sense of your audience, an organization, a tone — and your communicative purpose is what coordinates all of them, so it has to come first. One strategy writers use to find that purpose is to ask a simple question: "What should be different for my reader after they finish reading this?" — and whatever answer surfaces, even a rough one, becomes the seed everything else grows from. So here's the only move for right now: finish this sentence in whatever words come naturally — *Standardized testing is...* — and write what you actually believe, not what sounds polished. There's no wrong answer at this stage, because we're just finding out where you stand. Once you have that raw sentence down, we'll take it and shape it into a real thesis — a claim your reader can push back on.
